title: Shooting Stars and Meteorites
objective: After this level you can tell meteoroids, meteors and meteorites apart and explain meteor showers.
summary: A shooting star is a sand-grain meteoroid burning up. Meteor showers come from comet debris, like the August Perseids.

cards.headline: Most shooting stars are no bigger than a grain of sand.
cards.body: That bright streak you made a wish on was probably a speck about the size of a grain of sand. So how does a speck put on a light show?

cards.headline: Three names, one journey
cards.body: The same bit of space debris gets three names, depending on where it is. Floating in space, a small piece of rock or debris is a meteoroid. When it plunges into Earth's atmosphere and burns up, the streak of light is a meteor: the shooting star you see. If any piece survives to reach the ground, that piece is a meteorite. Handy test: the meteorite is the only one you could ever hold in your hand.

mascot.line: People swap these three names all the time. Where the debris is decides which name it gets.

cards.headline: Showers from comets
cards.body: Remember the comets from Level 53? They leave trails of debris behind. When Earth passes through a comet's trail of debris, you get a meteor shower, streak after streak. Most of those meteors come from particles about the size of a grain of sand. A few showers, like the Geminids, come from an asteroid instead. Either way, it's Earth driving through somebody else's dust.

cards.context: That's when Earth crosses the debris of Comet Swift–Tuttle. The trail stays put along the comet's path, and Earth reaches it at the same point in its orbit every year. So the Perseids are an annual appointment with a comet's leftovers.

cards.headline: Shooting stars: explained
learned: Meteor: the streak of light in our sky
Meteorite: a piece that reaches the ground
Showers come from comet debris trails

options.label: A meteor that is still in space
options.rationale: In space it’s called a meteoroid.

options.label: The streak of light in the sky
A piece that survives to reach the ground
A small comet with no tail
options.rationale: Meteorites are rock that reached Earth.

questions.explanation: A meteoroid in space becomes a meteor in the sky; any piece that reaches the ground is a meteorite.

options.label: Earth passing near the asteroid belt
options.rationale: Earth never passes through the asteroid belt.

options.label: Earth passing through a comet’s trail of debris
A comet crashing into the Moon
Stars falling toward Earth
options.rationale: Shooting stars aren’t stars at all.

questions.explanation: A comet leaves a trail of dust along its orbit. When Earth passes through it, many meteors streak across the sky.

questions.prompt: From Level 53: why does a comet leave a trail of debris that can later make meteors?

options.label: Near the Sun its ice turns to gas, and it leaves debris behind
Its tail breaks off every time it orbits
options.rationale: The trail is debris the comet leaves behind.

options.label: The solar wind grinds its rock into sand
options.rationale: The debris comes from the comet itself.

options.label: It collides with asteroids on each orbit
options.rationale: The trail comes from the comet itself.

questions.explanation: Comets are ice, dust and rock. Near the Sun the ice turns to gas, and the comet leaves a trail of debris; when Earth passes through it, you get a meteor shower.
